summary:
Anambra State stands under Nigeria's national framework. The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act applies nationwide and, per Human Rights Watch (October 2016), bans cohabitation between same-sex partners, any public show of a same-sex amorous relationship and the operation of gay organisations, carrying 10 to 14 years' imprisonment; the same reporting documents police torture and arbitrary arrests carried out under the statute.

Anambra lies in Nigeria's southeastern region and is outside the twelve northern states applying Shari'a criminal law, so the death-penalty provisions for sodomy under state Zina provisions do not reach this state. The applicable penalty for same-sex activity in Anambra is the secular southern figure of up to 14 years' imprisonment.

The UK Home Office country policy and information note on Nigeria (June 2025, updated April 2026) assesses that same-sex sex between men is criminalised under secular law with up to 14 years' imprisonment. The UK FCDO's travel advice for Nigeria, as relayed by Sahara Reporters (August 2026), warns of attacks, blackmail and intimidation against LGBT+ travellers and of up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex activity.

Police use the law against people for how they appear. TimesLIVE (March 2025) reports that a 24-year-old man, Okafor, was stopped by Lagos police, struck in the mouth with a police gun butt and freed only after paying almost half of the 50,000 naira bribe demanded, for 'looking gay'; those affected describe the SSMPA as a weaponised law creating a climate of hostility.

Dating applications carry a specific entrapment risk. Context/Thomson Reuters Foundation (April 2024) documents 'kito' gangs that lure LGBTQ+ Nigerians through Grindr and other apps to meetings where victims are beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing.

Enforcement takes the form of mass arrests at social venues. Wikipedia's country coverage records that 100-plus party-goers were arrested at a hotel in Asaba, Delta State, in June 2018; 57 young men at Egbeda, Lagos, in August 2018; the 'Warri 67' in Warri, Delta State, in August 2023; and 76 people arrested at a party in Gombe state in October 2023. These are raw counts from a national tally, not a per-capita ranking.

Cross-dressing has been proposed as a discrete offence. Reuters (September 2022) reports that transgender Nigerians fear proposals to criminalise cross-dressing.

Imprisonment of a prominent transgender woman raised placement questions that remain unresolved. Bobrisky (Idris Okuneye) pleaded guilty to four counts of Naira abuse on 5 April 2024 and was sentenced on 12 April 2024 to the maximum six months with no option of fine; she served the term in Kirikiri maximum-security prison, Lagos, and was released on 5 August 2024. Press coverage at sentencing openly asked which prison would hold 'the crossdresser', reflecting discretionary placement. An October 2024 investigative panel dismissed bribery allegations but found that placing her in a maximum-security prison violated the Nigerian Correctional Service Act because she was a first-time offender.

Care access is chilled by arrest and extortion risk. Many LGBTQ Nigerians fear seeking medical care or reporting crimes, and activists say the Same-Sex Marriage Prohibition Act hampers access to HIV prevention services and forces LGBTQ people and allies to abandon community health and education work.

A decade-outcome assessment of the statute exists. Context/Thomson Reuters Foundation (August 2024), marking ten years of the SSMPA, finds the 2014 law has fuelled violence, extortion and discrimination far beyond its scope and has effectively sanctioned abuse, with LGBTQ+ Nigerians reporting lost job prospects and increased attacks since it passed.
tangentialFactors:
Anambra's southeastern location places it outside the twelve Shari'a criminal-law states, so the death-penalty exposure that applies in northern Nigeria does not apply here; the operative risk in Anambra is the secular penalty of up to 14 years' imprisonment plus police extortion and violence.

The national pattern of mass arrests at social venues is documented by raw counts across several states (Asaba, Egbeda, Warri, Gombe), which track event size and policing activity rather than per-capita risk; no per-capita comparison between states is available from these figures.

In 2022 a court ruled Sections 4(1), 5(2) and 5(3) of the 2013 Act unconstitutional and unenforceable in any part of the country, though LGBTQ+ people still have no legal protections and face frequent violence.
localsOnly:
Anambra is a Nigerian state in the Southeastern region, Igbo-majority, formed in 1976, with capital Awka.

Residents of Anambra live under the full federal secular penalty regime for same-sex conduct, with no Shari'a provisions applying and no legal protections against discrimination or violence on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity.

Activists report that the Same-Sex Marriage Prohibition Act forces LGBTQ people and allies to abandon community health and education work, chilling resident-facing HIV prevention and outreach programmes.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether Anambra State has its own state-level enforcement operations, arrests, or legislative proposals on cross-dressing or gender presentation is not sourced in this inventory; the enforcement incidents cited are from other states and are illustrative of the national pattern only.

The 2022 court ruling striking down Sections 4(1), 5(2) and 5(3) of the 2013 Act is reported at country level; its precise effect on charges actually brought in Anambra is unresolved in these sources.

No Anambra-specific data on police extortion, 'kito' gang activity, or venue closures was identified; those findings are national or from other states.
